lead: An amplifier with negative feedback is stable only if its loop gain Aβ falls below 1 before the total loop phase reaches −180°. The loop gain is a complex number at every frequency, so stability is a question about a Bode plot, not a single number. This chapter reads the magnitude and phase of Aβ(jω), defines the two crossover frequencies, and turns them into gain margin and phase margin. These margins are checked in every op-amp circuit, audio power amplifier and control loop that must not self-oscillate.
prereq: You need: 4.1 and 4.2 for β and loop gain; Unit 3 for Bode plots, poles and cut-off frequencies.

sections.h3: Loop gain and the characteristic equation

blocks.text: Write the forward gain as A(s) and the feedback fraction as β(s). β is a pure number or a network ratio; it has no units. The loop gain is the gain around the complete loop, forward path times feedback path.

blocks.where: T(s) is the loop gain; A(s) is the forward gain; β(s) is the feedback fraction; s = jω = j2πf.

blocks.text: With negative feedback the closed-loop gain is A/(1 + T). The closed-loop poles are the roots of the characteristic equation.

blocks.where: T(s) is the loop gain; the roots of this equation are the closed-loop poles.

blocks.text: At β = 0 the closed-loop poles are the open-loop poles. Increasing β moves them. In a two-pole amplifier the closed-loop poles become complex and ring more as β rises, but they never cross the imaginary axis. With three or more poles they can cross into the right half plane when β is too large. That movement is the stability question. The open-loop Bode plot of T(jω) answers it because T is measured with the loop broken but correctly loaded. Deliberate positive feedback with |T| = 1 and ∠T = 0° is the oscillator case in 4.4.

sections.h3: Bode plot and the two crossings

blocks.text: A Bode magnitude plot draws 20 log₁₀|T| in dB against log f. Each pole adds a fall of 20 dB/decade above its cut-off frequency. Each zero adds a rise of 20 dB/decade. At a pole frequency the phase is −45°. Well above a pole the phase approaches −90°.

Two frequencies matter. The gain crossover frequency f_c is where |T| = 1, that is 0 dB. The phase crossover frequency f_180 is where ∠T = −180°. The margins are read at the opposite crossing: phase margin at f_c, gain margin at f_180.

blocks.where: PM is the phase margin in degrees; ∠T(jω_c) is the loop-gain phase at the gain crossover frequency where |T| = 1.
GM is the gain margin in dB; |T(jω_180)| is the loop-gain magnitude at the phase crossover frequency where ∠T = −180°.

blocks.text: A positive phase margin means the phase at f_c is above −180°. A positive gain margin means the magnitude at f_180 is below 1, that is below 0 dB. Negative margins mean the loop is unstable.

Phase margin measures how much extra phase lag the loop can take before the phase reaches −180° while |T| is still 1. A design target is 45° to 60°. Below about 30° the closed-loop response shows overshoot and ringing. A negative phase margin means oscillation.

Gain margin measures how much the loop gain can rise before the phase-crossover magnitude reaches 0 dB. One pole gives at most −90° of phase, so a one-pole loop is always stable and its gain margin is infinite on paper. Two poles can be made safe with 45° to 60° of phase margin. Three or more poles bring the phase near −180° or beyond, so such loops ring easily and need careful design.

Adding feedback moves the amplifier poles. That is why a Bode plot of the open-loop loop gain T answers a closed-loop stability question. In an op-amp datasheet the open-loop gain curve becomes T once you choose β with external resistors. Compensation networks that reshape this curve are covered in Unit 5.

figure.caption: The falling line is the loop gain of the worked example above 10 Hz. It crosses 0 dB at 10 kHz, where the phase margin is found.

spec.aria: Plot of the loop gain falling at 20 dB per decade and crossing the 0 dB line at 10 kHz.

examples.question: An amplifier has open-loop gain A₀ = 10⁵, poles at 10 Hz and 100 kHz, and β = 0.01. Find the low-frequency loop gain in linear and dB form, the gain crossover frequency, the phase margin and the gain margin.
steps: Low-frequency loop gain: A₀β = 10⁵ × 0.01 = 1000. In dB: 20 log₁₀(1000) = 60 dB.

Above 10 Hz the first pole makes |A| ≈ 10⁵/(f/10) = 10⁶/f. Set |Aβ| = 1, so |A| = 1/β = 100. Then 10⁶/f = 100, giving f = 10⁴ Hz = 10 kHz. This is below 100 kHz, so the second pole is small at the crossing.
Phase at 10 kHz: first pole gives about −90°. Second pole gives −arctan(10⁴/10⁵) = −5.7°. Total phase = −95.7°.
The phase approaches −180° only at infinite frequency, where |T| → 0. So the gain margin is infinite on paper.
examples.answer: Aβ at low frequency = 1000 (60 dB), gain crossover = 10 kHz, phase at crossover = −95.7°, phase margin = 84.3°, gain margin is infinite on paper.
examples.check:
import math
A0 = 1e5
beta = 0.01
f1 = 10.0
f2 = 1e5
T0 = A0*beta
T0_dB = 20*math.log10(T0)
fc = A0*f1*beta
phase = -90.0 - math.degrees(math.atan(fc/f2))
pm = 180.0 + phase
print(round(T0, 1))
print(round(T0_dB, 1))
print(round(fc, 1))
print(round(phase, 1))
print(round(pm, 1))

traps: Measuring gain margin at the gain crossover and phase margin at the phase crossover. Each margin belongs to the other crossing: PM at |T| = 1, GM at ∠T = −180°.
Forgetting the sign convention. A stable amplifier has positive gain margin because GM = −20 log|T| at the phase crossover. If |T| > 1 there, GM is negative.
Using the open-loop gain A₀ instead of the loop gain Aβ. β changes the gain crossover and therefore changes both margins.
Treating every pole as exactly −90° of phase at the crossover. A pole is −45° at its cut-off and approaches −90° only well above it.
Assuming infinite gain margin means no ringing. A two-pole loop can have infinite GM on paper and still ring badly if its phase margin is small.

quiz.q: Define gain crossover frequency and phase crossover frequency.
quiz.a: Gain crossover f_c is where |T| = 1, that is 0 dB. Phase crossover f_180 is where ∠T = −180°.

quiz.q: Why is gain margin measured at the phase crossover, not at the gain crossover?
quiz.a: Gain margin asks how much extra gain would push the loop to |T| = 1 at the frequency where the phase is already −180°. That frequency is the phase crossover.

quiz.q: A loop has low-frequency |T| = 80 dB and one pole at 100 Hz. Find the gain crossover frequency and phase margin.
quiz.a: 80 dB means |T| = 10⁴. A fall of 80 dB at 20 dB/decade is 4 decades. f_c = 100 Hz × 10⁴ = 1 MHz. A single pole gives about −90° at f_c, so PM = 180° − 90° = 90°.

quiz.q: A loop has poles at 1 kHz and 10 kHz. β is set so |T| = 1 at 5 kHz. Find the phase margin.
A loop has GM = +6 dB and PM = 20°. Is it stable? What problem do you expect?
quiz.a: It is stable by the positive gain margin, but the small phase margin predicts overshoot and ringing. Increase PM toward 45° to 60°.

quiz.q: State the usual design target for phase margin.
Why can a one-pole loop never reach −180° of phase?
quiz.a: One pole contributes at most −90° of phase. A finite one-pole loop stays between 0° and −90°, and approaches −90° only at infinite frequency.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, loop-gain simulation with a break in the feedback path is a standard check for op-amp, LDO and switching-regulator designs. Datasheets plot open-loop gain and phase so you can compute margins for your chosen feedback resistors. Control engineers use the same Bode margins for motor drives and power converters. Search for loop-gain simulation, phase margin in LDO datasheets, and Tian probe.
